papers.title: A Taxonomy of Numerical Differentiation Methods
papers.abstract: Differentiation is a cornerstone of computing and data analysis in every discipline of science and engineering. Indeed, most fundamental physics laws are expressed as relationships between derivatives in space and time. However, derivatives are rarely directly measurable and must instead be computed, often from noisy, potentially corrupt data streams. There is a rich and broad literature of computational differentiation algorithms, but many impose extra constraints to work correctly, e.g. periodic boundary conditions, or are compromised in the presence of noise and corruption. It can therefore be challenging to select the method best-suited to any particular problem. Here we review a broad range of numerical methods for calculating derivatives, present important contextual considerations and choice points, compare relative advantages, and provide basic theory for each algorithm in order to assist users with the mathematical underpinnings. This serves as a practical guide to help scientists and engineers match methods to application domains. We also provide an open-source Python package, PyNumDiff, which contains a broad suite of methods for differentiating noisy data.

papers.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.

papers.title: Direct Element-Level Mass Matrix Inversion
papers.abstract: Explicit finite element methods for transient solid dynamics commonly use lumped mass matrices to avoid solving systems of equations for nodal accelerations at each time step. However, diagonal mass matrices may inadequately represent inertia, particularly for higher-order elements and coarse or distorted meshes. This has limited the use of higher-order elements in explicit dynamic analyses. This paper presents a systematic method for directly evaluating the inverse of non-diagonal element-level mass matrices for solid isoparametric elements of arbitrary interpolation order. The method applies to mixed mass matrices defined as linear combinations of lumped and consistent mass matrices, with a weighting parameter controlling the transition between diagonal, consistent, and intermediate formulations. It therefore provides a framework for incorporating non-diagonal mass formulations, including those for quadratic elements, into explicit finite element algorithms. The approach is demonstrated by deriving an explicit inverse formula for the mixed mass matrix of the eight-node hexahedral element. This formula enables efficient element-level inversion without solving a global system. The proposed method can improve inertial representation in transient dynamic analyses while retaining the computational advantages of explicit time integration and is suitable for element-by-element implementations.

papers.title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
papers.abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.

papers.title: Beyond the error horizon: averaged quantile Kaczmarz methods for corrupted and noisy linear systems
papers.abstract: Linear systems and least-squares problems can contain measurement errors of different scales: a few measurements may be highly unreliable, while small noise affects every measurement. Residual-based iterative filtering can remove the influence of sparse corruption, but its accuracy is limited by a noise-dependent error horizon. We study how averaging and relaxation reduce this horizon in averaged quantile randomized Kaczmarz (AQRK), which filters equations by residual quantiles and averages a batch of single-row updates. Filtering, however, introduces an update bias that averaging alone cannot remove. We show that re-querying the accepted equations can remove this bias, and when the corruption is sparse enough relative to the conditioning of the matrix and large enough relative to the noise, we prove that AQRK with re-queried residuals reduces the horizon as averaging does without the corruption: its error decays to a horizon proportional to $\sqrt{\alpha/s}$, where $\alpha$ is the stepsize and $s$ the update batch size. Further, decreasing stepsizes or increasing batches gives convergence to the solution of the clean system. Numerical experiments support the theory and examine settings beyond it, including noise that cannot be re-queried and the corrupted low-rank tensor fitting problem. In the latter, AQRK inner solves succeed where standard alternating least-squares solvers and single-row robust updates fail.

papers.title: Convergence of discrete exterior calculus for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on surfaces
papers.abstract: We prove that discrete exterior calculus converges for the Hodge-Dirac and Hodge-Laplace problems on every closed oriented Riemannian surface. The proof applies the error bounds of a companion paper on finite element exterior calculus. We prove and use that every closed oriented surface, with any metric, carries uniformly regular families of triangulations that are acute with a uniform margin.

papers.title: High-Order Regularization for Singular and Nearly Singular Laplace and Stokes Layer Potentials in Two Dimensions
papers.abstract: Layer potentials represent the solutions of many elliptic boundary value problems, but their kernels have the singularity of the fundamental solution, so standard quadrature loses accuracy at targets on or near the boundary. In two dimensions, Gaussian regularization of the logarithmic kernel gives a smooth kernel involving the exponential integral $E_1$, but for the single layer its regularization error is only first order in the smoothing radius $\delta$. We construct modified kernels for two-dimensional Laplace and Stokes single- and double-layer potentials that achieve regularization error $O(\delta^p)$, $p=3,5,7$, uniformly for targets on and near the curve. The resulting method is both high-order accurate and easy to implement: the integrals are evaluated directly by the periodic trapezoidal rule on a single fixed set of boundary nodes for all targets. Choosing $\delta=c h^q$ with $q<1$, where $h$ is the node spacing, keeps the discretization error smaller than the regularization error as $h\to0$, and numerical experiments confirm the predicted $O(h^{pq})$ convergence. Finally, we combine the near-curve evaluation with a fast Poisson solver to compute the potentials on the entire Cartesian grid.

papers.title: A nonlinear multigrid method for the preconditioned lattice Boltzmann equation
papers.abstract: This work developed a preconditioned lattice Boltzmann equation (PLBE) smoother for the residual-driven full approximation scheme (FAS) multigrid to accelerate steady-state LBE calculations. To overcome the deterioration of LBE smoothing at low viscosity, we used a two- relaxation-time (TRT) collision model together with characteristic-velocity and kinetic precondition- ing to keep the relaxation frequency for the even-order moments within a favorable range, while independently selecting the relaxation frequency for the odd-order moments to reduce their local amplification factor. We further investigated F-, W-, and hybrid V/W-cycles to address residual stagnation observed with V-cycles at high Reynolds numbers. The 2D lid-driven cavity flow was used as a test case. At Re = 5000, TRT-PLBE-FAS achieves an approximately 27-fold speedup over single-grid TRT-PLBE. At Re = 20000 on a 20482 grid, the hybrid V/W-cycle reduces solution time by 14% compared with the W-cycle.

papers.title: Finite volume neural networks for singularly perturbed boundary value problems
papers.abstract: We develop a singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) methodology for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems. The proposed framework combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors, enabling stable and efficient approximation of sharp boundary variations induced by small perturbation parameters. Numerical experiments over a broad range of small perturbation parameters ($10^{-4}$ to $10^{-12}$), demonstrate that the sl-FVNN yields uniformly accurate predicted solutions and significantly improved convergence behavior compared to conventional FVNN methods. Further comparisons with sl-PINNs from (Gie, Hong, Jung, Appl. Anal. 2024) show that our sl-FVNNs attain comparable accuracy for reaction--diffusion and Burgers equations, while achieving significantly improved convergence for convection-dominated nonlinear problems. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating asymptotic layer structures into finite volume based neural networks, offering a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.

papers.title: Residual-driven lattice Boltzmann equation. Part I: framework and nonlinear solution methods
papers.abstract: We developed a residual-driven framework of the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) to integrate general nonlinear iterative methods. The nonlinear residual is constructed directly from the complete LBE collision-streaming update, allowing general nonlinear solvers to be integrated without modifying the original LBE algorithmic structure, i.e., the kernel consisting of collision-streaming, boundary conditions, and various forcing and interaction effects. Sophisticated techniques, such as weighted fixed-point iteration, full approximation scheme (FAS) multigrid, and Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov methods are integrated into the LBE via this framework, and preconditioned LBE is further incorporated as a nonlinear smoother to demonstrate solver composability. Numerical tests validate that FAS and Newton methods do converge to the same discrete steady fixed-point obtained with the primitive LBE iteration. For the 2D lid-driven cavity flow, the FAS scheme reduces the measured solution time by a factor of approximately 44 at Re = 1000 and more than 224 at Re = 5000. Accurate results are also obtained for the steady flows past a cylinder at Re = 20 and the NACA0012 airfoil at Re = 1000. The low Mach-number tests for the flow past a NACA0012 airfoil further show that both the FAS scheme and preconditioning can not only substantially reduce the work required to reach steady solutions, but also mitigate the zero Mach-number crisis.

papers.title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity
papers.abstract: High-order mesh r-adaptivity typically entails minimizing a nonlinear functional using its gradients and, for Newton-based methods, its Hessian. These derivatives can be expensive to derive, must be updated with any changes to the functional, and errors in the derivatives directly impact the convergence of r-adaptivity. Additionally, derivatives of the r-adaptivity operator are required for consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse problems. This work develops a framework for differentiable r-adaptivity based on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm. Given a pointwise functional defining the local mesh-adaptation objective, the proposed framework uses $\partial$FEM to automatically generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives. These local derivatives are then assembled into a global gradient vector and a Hessian operator through the finite element operator decomposition. The derivative kernels support portable CPU and GPU execution, with partial assembly and tensor sum factorization enabling matrix-free application of the Hessian operator. The framework also provides consistent sensitivities of the r-adaptivity operator through automatically generated mixed derivatives and implicit differentiation of the mesh stationarity equations. Numerical experiments show GPU solve times comparable to those of hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark problem, improvement in r-adaptivity convergence due to accurate computation of the derivatives, and demonstrate the use of mesh sensitivities for material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.

papers.title: Weak error estimates of a spectral Galerkin approximation to the stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough white noise
papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate weak error estimates for a spectral Galerkin approximation to a stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough space-time white noise. The roughness of the driving noise results that the mild solution possesses only $L^\infty$-regularity rather than any positive-order differentiability order regularity. The theory of classical numerical analysis reveals that the convergence rate of numerical solution is determined by the smoothness of the exact solution, and hence $L^\infty$-regularity is insufficient to yield any positive convergence rate. Indeed, De Vecchi et al.\ \cite{DeVecchi2026} studied a spectral Galerkin approximation to such equation and only proved pathwise convergence. However, we aim to derive positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation, which is determined by the roughness order of noise. To overcome the difficulty caused by the absence of smoothness of the exact solution, we turn to study the differentiability regularity of the first and second order Fr\'echet derivatives of the solution to a Kolmogorov equation associated with the spectral Galerkin approximation. We manage to prove that they possess nearly second order smoothness, enabling us to derive a positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation. Finally, we conduct a numerical experiment to illustrate the theortical analysis.

papers.title: B-Series Theory for Continuous Time Integration Methods
papers.abstract: B-Series are a common tool for constructing numerical integration methods and partitioned variations. In this paper, we expand the operations of B-Series to describe the formal expansion of modified differential equations found in multirate ODE solvers. Typically, such modified differential equations have time dependent approximations using summed fixed constant states. To create the B-Series we introduce a new operation called replacement to induce the constant states and add a time parameterization to the labels of the B-Series. By doing so we introduce new analysis via the permanent and block matrices which provide alternative formulations to composition and substitution. To support the time dependent labels properties are provided, the exact solution is described in Tree Iterated Integrals, and the underlying approximate representations are analyzed.

papers.title: An Explicit Parallelizable Robin-Robin Splitting Scheme for Navier-Stokes-Naghdi Shell Interaction
papers.abstract: We develop a novel explicit Robin-Robin splitting scheme for the system of an incompressible viscous fluid coupled to a time dependent Naghdi shell model. The shell model includes three displacement components and three independent rotation components, accounting for membrane, bending, and transverse-shear deformations. Both Robin conditions depend only on interface data from the previous time step, allowing the fluid and shell subproblems to be solved independently without coupling subiterations. For the fixed-domain Stokes-Naghdi problem, we derive a discrete energy identity that incorporates shell rotational inertia, interface velocities, and interface loads. We prove that the scheme is unconditionally stable for any fixed positive common Robin coefficient under homogeneous external data. Under suitable regularity and initialization assumptions, we establish first-order consistency and an $O(\sqrt{\Delta t})$ temporal error bound in the mechanical energy norm. Numerical experiments with a moving-domain pressure pulse compare the proposed scheme with the kinematically coupled $\beta$-scheme and a monolithic solver. To demonstrate its applicability to a more realistic vascular configuration, we simulate a stented artery using a bonded layered shell with stiff strut bands, capturing spatial variations in the arterial wall response.

papers.title: OCP: a greedy projection method for row-sparse representations of minimum-norm solutions
papers.abstract: In this paper, we propose a greedy projection method, termed orthogonal constraint pursuit (OCP), for identifying a small set of rows of a consistent linear system $Ax=b$ whose span contains the minimum-norm solution $x^*$, along with the coefficients of that representation. The method successively activates the most violated constraint, and then projects the iterate onto the intersection of all activated constraints. We prove that OCP is equivalent to OMP applied to the dictionary $A^T$ and the signal $x^*$, and that it terminates in at most rank(A) iterations. When $x^*$ is a linear combination of $s$ rows of a matrix whose rows are independent and uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, OCP identifies those rows in exactly $s$ iterations with probability $1-O(m^{-1})$, provided that $n\ge Cs\ln m$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$. We also derive a variant of OCP with constraint removal for hard-margin support vector machines with regularized bias, which returns the support vectors, along with the multipliers that satisfy the KKT conditions. Numerical results on both real and synthetic problems demonstrate the identification of representing rows and the regime in which it is competitive with Krylov subspace methods.

papers.title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
papers.abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

papers.title: A locking-free enriched linearized neural network for linear elasticity
papers.abstract: Neural-network Galerkin methods suffer from volumetric locking in nearly incompressible elasticity. We propose the locking-free enriched linearized neural network (LF-ENN), to the best of our knowledge, the first neural-network Galerkin method proved to be locking-free. Following the enriched Galerkin (EG) method of Yi, Lee and Zikatanov (2022), for finite $\lambda$ it admits a displacement-only formulation whose trial space is a linearized neural network enriched by one dilation field per element of an auxiliary mesh. The parameter $\lambda$ enters only through a piecewise constant discrete divergence, whose action on the dilation fields is the graph Laplacian of the dual graph of the mesh. Hence any conforming field can be made discretely divergence-free, and the error is bounded independently of $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$. The network needs no boundary factor: the Dirichlet condition is imposed weakly by Nitsche's method, and a Galerkin least-squares term on the shear part, as in ENN, together with a Hessian penalty on the elements along the traction boundary, replaces the trace inequality that networks lack. Under the stated approximation and quasi-uniformity assumptions, the discrete stability and error-estimate constants are independent of network width, mesh size, and $\lambda$, for both clamped and mixed boundary conditions. For solutions with reduced regularity, we establish an error estimate of order $h^s$ under the assumptions $u\in H^{1+s}(\Omega)^d$ and $p\in H^s(\Omega)$, with $s>1/2$. Numerical experiments, including Cook's membrane, demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in the presence of boundary singularities.

papers.title: Locking-free numerical methods for poroelasticity optimal control problems with minimal regularities
papers.abstract: We study distributed optimal control of a linear poroelastic system in a total pressure formulation, with displacement and fluid-pressure tracking and box constraints on the source control. A mechanical Schur complement gives well-posedness at zero storage for each fixed finite Lam\'e parameter, without estimates that grow like the inverse storage coefficient. We discretize the state and adjoint with conforming finite elements and dG(0) time stepping, and use piecewise constant controls. Under the stated regularity assumptions and a positive lower bound on storage, we prove first-order control and state error estimates uniform as the Lam\'e parameter increases. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence rates, examine the dependence on the Lam\'e and storage coefficients, and demonstrate localized pressure control with active bounds.

papers.title: A Divergence-Free Finite Element Discretization of a Convection-Cooling Optimal Control Problem
papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop and analyze a finite element discretization for a bilinear optimal control problem governed by a stationary convection-diffusion equation, in which an incompressible velocity field acts as the control through the convective term. Continuous piecewise linear finite elements are employed to approximate the state and adjoint variables, while the Stokes-type optimality equation for the velocity control is discretized by a low-order, pointwise divergence-free ($P_1^c\oplus RT_0-P_0$) finite element. To accommodate the nonconforming velocity space, we construct a discrete cost functional by replacing the continuous $H^1$-seminorm regularization with a suitable discrete velocity bilinear form and derive the corresponding discrete first-order optimality system. Since the bilinear coupling between the velocity control and the state variable renders the underlying optimization problem nonconvex, we establish local strong convexity of the discrete reduced cost functional under a second-order sufficient optimality condition at an isolated strict local minimizer of the continuous problem. Furthermore, by exploiting a divergence-preserving interpolation operator, auxiliary state and adjoint error estimates, and a stability relation between the discrete reduced-gradient residual and the control error, we derive a priori error estimates for the state, adjoint state and velocity control. Numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness of the optimized incompressible velocity in redistributing the temperature field and to verify the predicted convergence rates.

papers.title: For any wavenumber, the Helmholtz FEM matrix is invertible for almost all meshes
papers.abstract: We study invertibility of the conforming piecewise-linear Galerkin matrix for Helmholtz problems with a Dirichlet obstacle and the radiation condition approximated by \emph{either} impedance boundary condition \emph{or} a complex absorbing potential. We prove that for almost every simplicial mesh, and every fixed wavenumber, the Helmholtz FEM matrix with piecewise-linear elements is invertible.

papers.title: Anderson Acceleration of SCF Iteration and Newton's Method for Solving Nonlinear Eigenvector Problems
papers.abstract: The self-consistent field (SCF) iteration is a gateway method for solving nonlinear eigenvector problems, also known as nonlinear eigenvalue problems with eigenvector dependency (NEPv). However, the convergence of SCF can be slow in practice. In this paper, we study two local acceleration techniques for SCF applied to unitarily invariant NEPv: Anderson acceleration and Newton acceleration. A central difficulty in developing these techniques is the non-uniqueness of the eigenvector basis, which complicates direct application of standard Anderson acceleration and introduces singularity into the correction equation of the standard Newton formulation. For Anderson acceleration, we present three formulations based on unitarily invariant parameterization, basis alignment, and Grassmannian geometry, and establish regularity properties of the associated SCF maps. For Newton acceleration, we introduce basis-aligned updates and derive a correction equation whose operator is nonsingular under suitable assumptions, and prove local quadratic convergence. Numerical experiments on NEPv arising from computational physics and data analysis confirm the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed acceleration techniques.

papers.title: Convergence of a Parametric Symmetric Galerkin Boundary Element Method for the Mullins-Sekerka Flow
papers.abstract: We prove convergence of the fully discrete parametric scheme for the two-phase Mullins-Sekerka flow of a closed curve in the plane. The scheme combines piecewise linear parametric curves, a curvature discretization of Barrett--Garcke--N\"urnberg type and a symmetric Galerkin boundary element approximation of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. For a smooth solution whose curves satisfy a capacity condition, a uniform parameter mesh of size $h$, a constant time step $\tau$ and exact boundary element integrals, we show that the discrete curves stay regular and embedded, and that their distance to the exact curves in the topology $W^{1,\infty}$, after reparametrization by arclength, tends to zero in the first order of the time-step size $\tau$ whenever the mesh size $h$ is bounded by $c_0\tau^2$ for some $c_0$.

papers.title: Smoothing Bias and Direction Recovery at Boundary Minima of the Nuclear Norm along Matrix Lines
papers.abstract: We study optimal matrix directions associated with minimizing $\|G+\lambda\Theta\|_*$, the nuclear norm along a fixed affine line of real matrices with scalar multiplier $\lambda$. At a rank-deficient minimum, the compact polar factor can violate the tangency constraint even at the minimizing multiplier. Spectral smoothing gives a continuous scalar equation for tangency. We quantify its bias at a unique boundary minimum, where exactly one one-sided derivative vanishes. An orthogonal block decomposition shows that pseudo-Huber smoothing with scale $\delta$ shifts the multiplier by exact order $\delta^{2/3}$ as $\delta\to0$. The Frobenius error relative to the minimum-Frobenius-norm optimal direction has exact order $\delta^{1/3}$ when some singular values vanish at exactly second order in the multiplier displacement, and $\delta^{2/3}$ otherwise. A sharp rank bound rules out the slower rate when $\Theta$ has rank at most two. Huber smoothing gives an error of exact order $\delta$ for the same limiting direction. Convergent expansions in powers of $\delta^{1/3}$ also yield a three-scale extrapolation with $O(\delta)$ error after restoring feasibility.

papers.title: Residual-Driven Basis and Data Selection for Polynomial Approximation of High-Dimensional Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman Equations
papers.abstract: We develop greedy strategies for selecting global polynomial basis functions and training data in the sparse approximation of high-dimensional partial differential equations, with emphasis on Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations arising in nonlinear optimal control. Inspired by the goal-oriented dual-weighted residual framework, we derive a closed-form, mesh-free indicator that predicts, to first order, the reduction of the PDE residual obtained by adding a single candidate basis function, without solving an adjoint problem. In the data-driven regime, we jointly select basis functions and gradient-augmented training samples by maximizing the predicted decrease of a supervised loss. Numerical experiments on benchmark PDEs and nonlinear optimal control problems in up to 35 dimensions show accuracy comparable to non-adaptive approaches with substantially fewer basis functions and training samples.

papers.title: A singularity detecting uniformly convergent quantum wavelet framework for weakly singular nonlocal Emden--Fowler systems with quantum Mittag--Leffler sources
papers.abstract: We develop a quantum wavelet-based computational framework for coupled systems of Caputo-type quantum ($q$-) fractional Emden--Fowler problems with $q$-Mittag--Leffler source terms, where the solutions exhibit singular behavior in time. Here $q\in(0,1)$ denotes the parameter of $q$-calculus. The highest-order Caputo $q$-fractional derivatives are expanded through the Haar wavelet basis, and the lower-order fractional derivatives are approximated through Jackson $q$-fractional integrals of Haar wavelets. The continuous problem reduces to a nonlinear algebraic system on the midpoint collocation points. Under suitable structural assumptions, the Banach fixed-point theorem yields the existence and uniqueness of the continuous solutions and wellposedness of the discrete solutions on collocation points. The nonlinearity of the given problem is dealt with by the damped Newton's iteration. In addition, We prove stability of the scheme and derive rigorous convergence estimates in a weighted norm that remains uniformly controlled despite the appearance of singular weight at $t=0$ in the continuous model. When the highest-order fractional derivatives are H\"older continuous with exponent $\sigma$, the mathematical error of weakly singular solution and its lower-order fractional derivatives become $\mathcal{O}(\tau_L^{\sigma})$, where $\tau_L=2^{-(L+1)}$ denotes the width of the finest subintervals for maximum level of resolution $L$. First-order convergence is guaranteed under stronger regularity with $\sigma=1$. Several test cases are considered to confirm the accuracy and robustness of the present approach, which strongly agrees with the theoretical estimates. In particular, first-order convergence is observed even where the stronger regularity assumption is not satisfied.

papers.title: Right shape, wrong time: phase errors of ODE solvers in the flame problem
papers.abstract: The flame model $y'=y^2-y^3$, $y(0)=\delta$, is a standard illustration of stiffness: for $\delta=10^{-4}$ the stiff MATLAB solvers ode23s and ode15s need only 99 and 140 steps, against 3040 for ode45. We show that these cheap solutions have the right shape at the wrong time: they place the front 29 and 329 time units early, with maximal errors 0.95 and 1.00. Because all solutions are time translates of one master profile, the global error of every numerical solution with values in $[\delta,1)$ is exactly a phase error, $y_k=y_\delta(t_k-D_k)$. For fixed-step one-step methods of order $p$ we prove $D=h^p\int_\delta^{y}g+O(h^{p+1})$ with a remainder bounded uniformly in $\delta$, so that the delay grows at most like $h\ln(1/\delta)$ for $p=1$ and stays bounded for $p\geq2$. For any computed solution the delay is exactly the sum of its defects with respect to the exact flow, converted into time; a heuristic model, confirmed by MATLAB runs, explains why it is created in the first few steps and why tightening the tolerances is an expensive cure. Integrating for $1/y$, which runs like a clock in the slow phase, with an absolute tolerance reduces the error by several orders of magnitude, at a median cost close to that of the standard formulation. The mechanism needs only that the equation is autonomous; its general form is the subject of a companion paper.

papers.title: Finite element nonlinear nudging for the Navier-Stokes equations
papers.abstract: Nonlinear nudging augments the classical linear nudging (continuous data as- similation) term with a nonlinear feedback that strengthens as the observed error decreases, and yields super-exponential convergence to the true state. In this paper, we study nonlinear nudging for the 3-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with the finite element method, which allows complex geometries and physical boundary conditions. We propose an implicit-explicit (IMEX) finite element scheme with inf-sup stable elements, prove its unconditional long-time stability, and show for the spatially semi-discrete scheme that the error reaches a prescribed tolerance in finite time. Our analysis also suggests that the non- linear nudging term requires the mesh resolution to be fine enough (${\chi = O(H^{-1})}$, where ${\chi}$ is the nonlinear nudging intensity and ${H}$ is the observation mesh size). Further, our error estimates suggest that a larger nonlinear exponent ${\gamma}$ requires finer observational resolution, which is confirmed by numerical tests. Numerical experiments, including two-dimensional forced viscous flow in a periodic box, flow past a cylinder, and flow over a flat plate, show that nonlinear nudging synchronizes with the true solution considerably faster than linear nudging. We also show that observations in a subregion suffice to synchronize the whole flow

papers.title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity
papers.abstract: We develop neural network methods for the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at a small viscosity $\varepsilon > 0$, whose accuracy is uniform in $\varepsilon$ and whose residual is evaluated on a grid that does not resolve the vorticity boundary layer. In the vorticity-stream function formulation with the slip boundary conditions, a vorticity layer of width $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ forms along the walls. The trial function of the singular layer Physics-Informed Neural Network (sl-PINN) contains the corrector of the asymptotic analysis, together with the law that fixes its amplitude at the wall. The amplitude is tied to the wall trace of the network itself, so that the method requires no a priori knowledge of the limit solution. The sl-PINN keeps the error uniform in $\varepsilon$ over six decades, for the Stokes and the Navier-Stokes equations alike, although in the latter the wall trace travels with the flow and is not known in advance. An enrichment that uses the thin scale but leaves the profile and the amplitude of the layer free deteriorates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Since the corrector carries the layer analytically, the Laplacian in the residual can be discretized by a finite volume flux difference on a coarse grid. The resulting singular layer Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) attains the same uniform accuracy as the sl-PINN, to within the scatter of the random seed, at about half the cost of a training step. The combination of the asymptotic corrector with the coarse-grid finite volume discretization is the main result of this article.

papers.title: Decision Stability and Model Reduction for Hamilton--Jacobi Navigation in Multiscale Flows
papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles plan time-optimal routes through flow fields that are known only through reduced, finite-resolution models of an underlying multiscale flow. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi homogenization concerns convergence of the value function as the fine scale vanishes; but what a vehicle commits to is a route, and value accuracy need not imply route accuracy. We study this gap for a fixed-resolution reduction rather than in the homogenization limit. The committed route's dependence on the model-reduction error splits into two regimes. When the optimal route is a unique, nondegenerate minimizer with a regular value-function neighborhood, it depends Lipschitz-continuously on the reduction error, while the extra travel time from acting on the reduced model grows only quadratically with that error. When two routes are tied on the cut locus of the value function, the value remains stable, but an arbitrarily small change in the flow can switch the selected route, making route selection discontinuous in the reduction error. This dichotomy identifies where a reduced model must be accurate: not where the flow error is largest, but where the route choice is fragile. In the regular regime it yields a resolution-allocation principle, while an oracle marginal-regret benchmark illustrates the potential benefit of decision-aware resolution allocation relative to refinement based on flow-error magnitude.

papers.title: Multilevel Filtering on Manifolds with Light Schr\"odinger Bridges
papers.abstract: In this article we consider the filtering of partially observed diffusions when the observations, made at discrete times, are noiseless. Each observation then confines the hidden state to a manifold defined by the data, whose type, for instance a sphere or an affine subspace, may change from one observation time to the next. In practice, the filter is approximated by particle filters, which require the diffusion to be discretized in time. Multilevel Monte Carlo reduces the cost of this discretization only if the particle approximations at consecutive discretization levels stay close, which standard particle filters do not ensure. We develop a new particle filter based on light Schr\"odinger bridges, which works between changing manifolds and can be coupled across discretization levels. A key insight is that the previous state enters the light Schr\"odinger bridge only through a few features, so that the bridge only has to be fitted on the new manifold, regardless of the type of the previous one. We bound the bias of this particle filter and the gap between its approximations at consecutive levels, and show numerically, on spheres and on manifolds that change type, that this gap is much smaller than with standard multilevel particle filters, and that, with the cost of the fits included, a hybrid estimator that uses it at the fine levels reduces the cost at small tolerances.
